Imagine two people who make the same mistake. The first person sees it wasn't
my fault. The tools were bad. No one told me. The instructions weren't clear. The
second person says, I could have asked more questions. I should have checked my
work. I'll correct it and do better next time. Which person do you think will grow
faster? The second person. Why? Because they focus on what they can control. This
is called extreme ownership. Extreme ownership means taking responsibility
for your actions, your attitude and your response. It does not mean everything is
your fault and it does not mean blaming yourself for things outside your
control. It means asking, what can I do to make this better? What can I learn? What
is the best next step? People who grow ask these questions regularly. Sometimes
things genuinely are not your fault. A supplier is late. The weather changes. A
machine breaks. Someone forgets to give you important information. Those things
happen. But even when you cannot control what happened, you can control what you
do next. You can complain. You can blame. You can wait for someone else to solve
the problem. Or you can ask, what is the best next step? People who take ownership
look for solutions. They do not waste their energy searching for someone to
blame. They use that energy to communicate, to solve and to move forward. Here is a
simple example. Your manager asks for a report by Friday. On Wednesday, you
realize you are falling behind. One person stays quiet. They hope the problem will
disappear. Friday arrives and the report is still not finished. Another person
speaks up on Wednesday and says, I'm running behind. Can you help me prioritize?
Here is what I have completed and here is what is still missing. Which person is
easier to trust? The second person. Taking ownership means communicating early. It
means not hiding problems. Bad news does not improve because you keep it quiet. A
small problem shared early can often be solved. A hidden problem usually becomes
a bigger problem. Imagine you are building a fence. You take a measurement but
something does not look right. You could ignore it. You could continue and hope it
works out. Or you could stop, ask a question and check the measurement again.
That takes ownership. A small conversation today can prevent a large
mistake tomorrow. Ownership is often visible in small moments. When you ask
instead of guessing. When you check instead of hoping. When you speak up instead of
staying silent. When you fix instead of hiding. At our company, we do not expect
perfection. Everyone makes mistakes. Everyone misses something occasionally.
What matters is what happens next. Do you hide the mistake? Do you make excuses? Do
you wait for someone else to discover it? Or do you admit it? Learn from it and help
fix it. People respect honesty. They respect people who take responsibility and they trust
people who tell the truth early. Here is another important point. Ownership is contagious. When
one person takes responsibility, other people often begin to do the same. The conversation
changes. Instead of asking, who caused this? The team begins asking, how do we solve this?
Instead of protecting themselves, people begin supporting one another. And as that
happens, the whole team becomes stronger. Remember this sentence. Excuses stop growth.
Ownership creates growth. Excuses keep your attention on the past. Ownership moves your
attention toward the future. Excuses ask, whose fault is this? Ownership asks,
what can I do now? The second question will always move you forward. The next time something goes
wrong, pause for a moment. Notice your first reaction. You may feel frustrated. You may want
to defend yourself. You may want to explain why the problem was not your fault. That reaction is
normal. But you do not have to stay there. You can take a breath and ask, what part of this can I
influence? What action can I take? Who needs to know? What can I learn for next time? These
questions create progress and the more often you ask them, the more natural ownership becomes.
So this week, practice extreme ownership. If something goes wrong, do not look for excuses
first. Look for your next action. Ask questions. Check your work. Communicate early. Fix problems.
Learn from mistakes. Support your teammates. And keep moving forward. Because people who
take ownership become people who are trusted. Trusted people are given greater responsibility.
And people who handle responsibility well become leaders. Extreme ownership does not begin with
the title. It begins with a choice. The choice to stop blaming. The choice to start acting.
And the choice to ask, what can I do now?

Have you ever spent an hour doing something, only to discover that someone else could do
it in 10 minutes?
That happens to all of us.
Sometimes we work hard, but we are using a slow method.
Sometimes we repeat mistakes that another person has already learned how to avoid.
One of the fastest ways to grow is to stop assuming that your way is the best way.
Instead, ask one simple question.
Who already does this better than me?
That question can save time.
It can prevent mistakes, and it can help you improve much faster.
This is called benchmarking.
Benchmarking means finding an excellent example and learning from it.
It means studying what works, understanding why it works, and using those lessons to improve
your own performance.
It does not mean copying without thinking.
It means learning intelligently.
The best people in the world do not know everything.
They know how to learn.
Think about professional athletes.
And the greatest athletes still have coaches.
The greatest musicians still have teachers.
Successful business leaders still ask for advice.
Why?
Because excellence leaves clues.
When someone achieves excellent results, they are usually doing certain things consistently.
If you observe those things, you can learn from them.
If someone has already solved a problem, their experience can become your shortcut.
Maybe someone on your team writes clearer emails.
Ask them how they structure the message.
Maybe someone organizes files better.
Ask them to show you their system.
Maybe someone is excellent with customers.
Listen to the questions they ask.
Notice their tone.
Watch how they respond when something goes wrong.
Often.
The best example is already close to you.
It may be a teammate, a manager, a supplier, or someone with more experience.
The important question is, what can I learn from the way they do this?
AI can also help you benchmark your work.
Before sending an email, ask.
Can this be clearer?
Before creating a document, ask.
Can this be simpler?
Before solving a problem, ask.
Is there a better method?
Before finishing a task, ask.
What might I have missed?
These small questions create major improvements over time.
They help you notice gaps.
They help you compare your first version with a stronger version.
And they help you improve before the work reaches the customer.
But there is something important to remember.
Benchmarking requires humility.
Pride says, I already know.
Humility says, teach me.
Pride protects the current method.
Humility looks for a better one.
Pride stops learning.
Humility keeps growing.
There is no shame in asking for help.
In many situations, asking for help is a sign of good judgment.
It shows that the result matters more than your ego.
And it shows that you respect the experience of others.
Imagine two people building the same table.
The first person begins immediately.
They do not ask questions.
They do not look at an example.
They simply start.
The second person spends five minutes speaking with an experienced carpenter.
They ask about the measurements.
They ask about the correct tools.
They ask which mistakes to avoid.
The first person works for four hours and makes several mistakes.
The second person works for three hours and produces a better table.
Which person was more productive?
The second person.
Why?
Because learning first saved time later.
Five minutes of learning saved an hour of work.
That is the power of benchmarking.
Here is another example.
You are creating an important presentation.
You could guess what good looks like or you could study a strong presentation.
You could ask someone skilled to review your work.
Five minutes of useful feedback could improve the entire result.
That is benchmarking.
It is finding the standard before you finish the work.
When you know what excellence looks like, you can compare your work with it.
